A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LadderSym and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Renumbered and relocated material can be matched reliably. Internal reporting inconsistencies do not prevent comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original LadderSym benchmark results, encoder probes, fusion and input ablations, attention analyses and statistical comparisons.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds a curated beginner-performance evaluation, latency measurements and error-specific attention analysis.

M1.justification: The interleaved encoder, alternating cross-attention and additive fusion, symbolic decoder prompting, architecture sizes and training objective remain unchanged. The prompt-token specification adds documentation; annotation assistance and suggested future pre-alignment do not establish changes to the detector.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained MAESTRO-E and CocoChorales-E benchmarks and v1's linked real-playing demos, v2 introduces a curated evaluation of unscripted beginner-piano mistakes from three performers (§4.1, §A.7). This substantially expands the documented evaluation population and error conditions. The text and Table 9 describe 20 pieces, although Table 8 inconsistently lists 10 tracks.

E2.justification: The synthetic accuracy comparisons retain Polytune and the same MT3/DTW baseline, renamed Explicit Align. The efficiency comparison expands from LadderSym versus Polytune in v1 to include Ladder in v2 Table 3. The new real-data table reports only LadderSym and Polytune.

E3.justification: v2 adds a held-out real-performance evaluation without finetuning and separately reports encoder, first-decoder-token and worst-case-token latency. Existing synthetic training budgets, preprocessing, probes and 50 ms note-matching tolerance remain unchanged. The new dataset's precise sample count is inconsistently documented as 10 versus 20.

E4.justification: v2 adds an explicit synthetic-to-real robustness evaluation without finetuning (§A.7), extending validation beyond the existing synthetic ablations and linked demos. Figure 9 additionally tests whether missed, wrong and flipped notes produce distinctive first-layer attention patterns, finding similar diagonal structures. Existing fusion/input ablations, probes and layerwise attention analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The new latency table reports values with plus/minus quantities, adding uncertainty reporting absent from v1's latency summary. Their statistical meaning and measurement counts are unspecified. The paired t-tests, Wilcoxon tests, Bonferroni threshold and training seed 365 remain unchanged; no increase in repeated training runs is documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds per-piece real-data results: Table 9 reports missed-note F1 of 78.5% versus Polytune's 63.9%, and extra-note F1 of 81.6% versus 80.6%. It replaces v1's 124/147 ms-per-token summary with different latency measures, so these are not directly comparable speed changes. Most synthetic F1 results remain unchanged, but the one-joint-layer extra-note entry changes from 46.40% to 46.80%, and LadderSym's CocoChorales-E missed/extra entries in the ablation table change from 61.4/61.7 to 61.7/61.4. Table 2's precision and recall results are removed.

T1.justification: The encoder equations, fusion expression and synthetic error-generation algorithm and distributions are retained. Neither version presents new theoretical results or proofs. Added repetition and reversal examples explain the existing error taxonomy.

C1.justification: The architectural contributions and synthetic-performance claims remain, but v2 adds prominent claims of generalization to genuine beginner mistakes and practical utility. It also claims a first/largest public beginner-error dataset and positions LadderSym as an annotation assistant for expanding real-world training data, substantially broadening the contribution scope.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the discussion of acoustic/timbre generalization and associated augmentation/licensing difficulties with specific limitations involving dense-note masking, segment-boundary errors and large tempo differences. It adds interpretations of real-data performance, annotation-assisted dataset creation and the absence of error-specific attention geometry (§A.9.3). These materially revise applicability boundaries and mechanism explanations.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the shared prompt/output vocabulary and Correct labels in symbolic prompts, explicitly states instrument macro-averaging, and documents digital-piano/VST recording and model-assisted annotation verified by two reviewers. It supplies a LadderSym code-repository link where v1 promised public release upon acceptance. Core hyperparameters, software, hardware and seed information are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting tutoring, feedback, annotation assistance and temporal multimodal positioning, including Sigrist, Apaydınlı, Kirillov, Monarch and Qwen2.5-Omni. Several broad multimodal examples and original dataset references disappear. Section 2.2 sharpens comparisons with compressed conditioning and assumed temporal alignment, while the principal explicit-versus-latent alignment positioning remains.

P1.justification: The introduction, related-work explanations, method introduction and results narrative undergo substantial rewriting. Appendix training and metrics become standalone sections, instrument results move, and the NeurIPS checklist is removed. v2 adds an appendix roadmap, acknowledgments, a reproducibility statement and a manuscript-editing disclosure, alongside the conference-format conversion.

P2.justification: Table 2 is substantially redesigned into a compact F1-only comparison. v2 adds latency, prompt-token and real-performance tables plus Figure 9, and restructures the dataset summary with provenance and comparison rows. Existing architecture and attention figures are largely retained, with caption, labeling and placement changes throughout the conference layout.

improvement.justification: The real-performance evaluation adds useful quantitative validation beyond v1's synthetic benchmarks and linked demos, while prompt documentation and concrete failure conditions improve clarity. These gains are limited by the small, clean digital-piano setting and reporting problems: Table 8 lists 10 tracks versus 20 elsewhere, and §A.7.2 inconsistently claims both halved labeling time and threefold throughput. Removed precision/recall results also reduce diagnostic detail. Overall, the added evidence supports a limited net improvement.
